title: The perfect passive and the perfect participle

objectives.can: Recognise the perfect passive participle and read it with sum as a perfect passive tense.

explanation.summary: The perfect passive is the first Latin tense made of two words: a perfect participle and a form of sum. The participle is an adjective, so it changes its ending to match the subject. The same participle, alone, is one of the commonest ways of saying 'having been done' in the Vulgate.

sections.heading: Two words, one tense
body: The present, imperfect and future passives of the last lesson are single words. The perfect passive is not. It is a perfect passive participle together with a form of *sum*: *traditus est*, 'he was handed over, he has been handed over'.

The participle carries the meaning and the voice. The form of *sum* carries person, number and the time. With *est* or *sunt* the tense is the perfect passive; with *erat* or *erant* it is the pluperfect passive ('had been …'); with *erit* it is the future perfect passive.
Latin often puts the two words apart, and either may come first: *inventus est* and *est inventus* mean the same. Read the participle first, then look for the form of *sum*.

sections.heading: The participle is an adjective
body: The perfect passive participle ends in -tus, -ta, -tum (or -sus, -sa, -sum), declined like *bonus*, *bona*, *bonum*. Like any adjective it agrees with the word it describes in case, number and gender. When it forms a tense, that word is the subject, so the ending depends on the subject: -tus for a masculine singular subject, -ta for feminine, -tum for neuter, -ti, -tae, -ta in the plural.

This is why a Latin text shows both *traditus est* and, with a feminine or plural subject, forms such as *data est* and *dicta sunt*. The part that changes is the participle; *est* and *sunt* follow the number of the subject.

sections.heading: What the perfect passive means
body: The tense reports an action as done, and with the present *est* it is translated either 'was done' or 'has been done', just as the perfect active covers both. *judicatus est* in John 3 is 'he has been judged'; *traditus est* in Romans 4 is 'he was handed over'. The sense is fixed by the context.

A perfect participle used by itself is 'having been done' or just 'done', a description of a person or thing that has undergone the action. *Baptizatus Jesus* is 'Jesus, having been baptized' and the participle sits beside the subject without any form of *sum*.

sections.heading: Other forms of sum in the Vulgate
body: Besides *est* and *erat* the Vulgate and later Latin often use the perfect forms of *sum* with the participle: *fuit* and *fuerat*. The sense is usually the same as the plain forms: in John 3 the form *fuerat* with the participle gives a pluperfect, 'had been sent'. Do not count on a difference of tense where the context gives none.

sections.heading: Reading the library's tags
body: The analysis in the library is automatic. It tags these participles as Tense=Perf, Voice=Pass, VerbForm=Part, with Case, Number and Gender. Many endings are ambiguous (for example -a can be nominative feminine singular or neuter plural), and the exercises use only the words the analyser read with a single clear reading. When the learner meets a participle whose case seems wrong, the ending may have fooled the analyser, not the learner.

misunderstandings: *est* in *traditus est* is not 'is' standing by itself: it is a helper, and the two words together are one past tense. Do not translate it as 'is handed over' (that is *traditur*).
The participle does not agree with the nearest noun. It agrees with the subject of the tense, which may be at the other end of the sentence.

Not every participle ending in -tus is passive. Deponent verbs have perfect participles that look the same and are active in meaning; the corpus tags them as active. They are taught in a later lesson.

deeper.heading: Why the participle is called perfect
body: The name refers to completed action: the participle describes something already done by the time of the main verb. English has the same idea in 'having been baptized'. Latin has no perfect participle for the active voice, so a Latin writer who wants 'having done' often uses an ablative absolute or a deponent verb, both of which come later in the course.

examples.analysis: *traditus* is the perfect passive participle of *trado*, nominative singular masculine. With *est* it forms the perfect passive: 'was handed over'. Both words are needed; neither alone says 'was handed over'. The next verb, *resurrexit*, is perfect active and runs on in the same past time.

examples.analysis: *inventus est*, 'he was found' or 'he has been found', is a perfect passive. The subject is masculine singular, so the participle is *inventus*. The earlier verbs in the verse are in the pluperfect: the sentence reports first what had happened, and then the new state of affairs.

examples.analysis: A pair that should be learned together. *judicatur* is present passive: 'is judged'. *judicatus est* is perfect passive: 'has been judged'. The verb is the same and the voice is the same; what differs is the tense, and in the second case the tense takes two words.

The first is active; the second and third are passive

check.explain: judicatur is one word, present passive: 'is judged'. judicatus est is a participle with est, perfect passive: 'has been judged'. The voice is the same in both; only the tense changes.
